title: Gradient: velocity and acceleration
learning_outcomes: Explain why the gradient of a displacement-time graph gives velocity.
Explain why the gradient of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration.
Calculate positive, zero and negative gradients from straight graph sections.
Use a tangent to estimate an instantaneous velocity or acceleration on a curve.
State the correct units and interpret the sign of a graph-derived result.
prior_knowledge_summary: From 9702_t02_cm02_l03, students can distinguish displacement-time and velocity-time graphs and read their coordinates, signs and qualitative motion states.
Students recognise stationary motion, constant velocity, changing velocity and reversal without using gradient calculations.
new_learning: Gradient is vertical change divided by horizontal change.
The gradient of a displacement-time graph gives velocity.
The gradient of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration.
A tangent gives the instantaneous gradient of a curve at one point.
The sign and unit of a gradient identify the direction and physical quantity.
not_yet_taught: Finding displacement or distance from area under a velocity-time graph
Constructing one motion graph from another

mapped_demands: Calculate acceleration from a straight velocity-time graph.
Estimate instantaneous acceleration from a tangent to a curved velocity-time graph.

knowledge_boundary: This lesson calculates and interprets gradients of displacement-time and velocity-time graphs. It does not use areas under graphs, construct translated graphs or use constant-acceleration equations.

blocks.title: Two cyclists, one glance
body: Two displacement-time lines start together. One rises gently and one rises steeply.
Prediction: which cyclist has the greater velocity, and how could a number prove it?
Lesson 3 let us say both move in the positive direction. Today we turn steepness into a measured velocity.

figure.purpose: Create a need for a numerical measure of graph steepness.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn displacement-time axes with two straight lines from the origin, one gentle and one steep. Add cyclist icons A and B but no gradient triangles or answers.
figure.alt_text: Two displacement-time lines rise from the origin with different steepness.

blocks.title: Gradient measures change per unit time
body: Choose two well-separated points on a straight graph section.
Find the vertical change and the horizontal change using final value minus initial value.
Gradient = vertical change / horizontal change.
A large gradient magnitude means the vertical quantity changes rapidly. The sign records whether it increases or decreases as time passes.

figure.purpose: Show the rise-over-run construction without tying it to only one motion quantity.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn generic quantity-time straight line with two points and a large right-angled triangle. Label vertical change and time change. Show final minus initial beside each change.
figure.alt_text: A large triangle on a straight graph section shows vertical change divided by time change.

blocks.title: Why displacement-time gradient is velocity
body: On a displacement-time graph, vertical change is change in displacement and horizontal change is change in time.
Its gradient is therefore change in displacement divided by change in time.
That ratio is velocity. A positive gradient gives positive velocity, a negative gradient gives negative velocity and zero gradient gives zero velocity.
blocks.remember: Formula to remember: velocity = gradient of a displacement-time graph.

blocks.title: Resolve the cyclists
body: Cyclist A changes displacement from 2 m to 14 m while time changes from 1 s to 5 s.
vertical change = 14 - 2 = 12 m and horizontal change = 5 - 1 = 4 s.
velocity = gradient = 12 / 4 = +3.0 m s^-1.
Cyclist B changes displacement by 20 m in the same 4 s, so its velocity is +5.0 m s^-1. B has the steeper line and greater velocity.

figure.purpose: Model a fully annotated straight-line displacement-time calculation and comparison.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn paired displacement-time lines A and B with large calculation triangles spanning 1 s to 5 s. Put coordinate values on axes and a compact rise-over-run layout beside the graph.
figure.alt_text: Two displacement-time lines with annotated triangles give velocities of positive 3.0 and positive 5.0 metres per second.

blocks.title: Why velocity-time gradient is acceleration

symbols.Delta v: change in velocity in m s^-1, equal to final velocity minus initial velocity

body: On a velocity-time graph, vertical change is change in velocity and horizontal change is change in time.
The gradient is Delta v / Delta t, exactly the acceleration formula.
Its units are (m s^-1) / s = m s^-2.
blocks.remember: Acceleration = gradient of a velocity-time graph.

blocks.title: Read the sign as direction of change
body: A velocity-time line that rises has positive gradient, so acceleration is positive.
A line that falls has negative gradient, so acceleration is negative.
A horizontal line has zero gradient, so acceleration is zero even when velocity is non-zero.
This matches Lesson 2: negative acceleration describes a negative change in velocity, not automatically slowing down.

figure.purpose: Compare positive, zero and negative velocity-time gradients and their acceleration signs.
figure.brief: Three-row hand-drawn comparison: rising velocity-time line, horizontal line and falling line. Pair each with positive, zero or negative acceleration and a small change-in-velocity arrow.
figure.alt_text: Rising, horizontal and falling velocity-time lines correspond to positive, zero and negative acceleration.

blocks.title: Why the steepest-looking line may not win
body: It feels safe to compare line angles by eye. That works only when the graph scales are identical.
Stretching an axis changes the drawn angle without changing the motion.
Use coordinate changes and units. Compare calculated gradient magnitudes, not page angles.

figure.purpose: Expose the danger of comparing visual angle across differently scaled axes.
figure.brief: Two small graphs show the same coordinate data with differently stretched axes, making the line angles look different. Include matching coordinate labels but no conclusion banner.
figure.alt_text: The same coordinate data looks steeper on one graph because its axes use a different scale.

blocks.title: A curve needs a tangent
body: A curve has a changing gradient, so two points on the curve give only an average over an interval.
To estimate the instantaneous value at one point, draw a tangent that just touches the curve there and follows its local direction.
Choose two widely separated points on the tangent, not two nearby points on the curve. Then calculate the tangent's gradient.
On a displacement-time curve this gives instantaneous velocity. On a velocity-time curve it gives instantaneous acceleration.

figure.purpose: Teach correct tangent placement and point selection for an instantaneous gradient.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn curved velocity-time graph with point P, one tangent touching at P and a large triangle whose two chosen points lie on the tangent. Add a faint incorrect chord for contrast, clearly crossed out.
figure.alt_text: A tangent touches a velocity-time curve at point P and a large triangle on the tangent is used for its gradient.

blocks.title: Estimate an instantaneous acceleration
body: A tangent to a velocity-time curve at 6.0 s passes through convenient points (2.0 s, 5.0 m s^-1) and (10.0 s, 17.0 m s^-1).
a = Delta v / Delta t = 12.0 / 8.0 = +1.5 m s^-2.
The positive sign means acceleration in the chosen positive direction.

blocks.title: A reliable gradient routine
items: Identify the graph and the physical quantity represented by its gradient.
For a curve, draw a tangent at the required point.
Choose two far-apart points on the straight section or tangent.
Calculate vertical change and horizontal change as final minus initial.
Divide, attach the correct unit and interpret the sign.

blocks.title: Return to the cyclists
body: The steeper displacement-time line represented the cyclist with the greater velocity because its displacement changed more each second.
Gradient turns that visual clue into a measured rate.
The same idea works one level later: change of velocity per second is acceleration, so it appears as velocity-time gradient.

requirements: Use large readable triangles and well-separated coordinate points.
Vary comparison, annotated calculation and tangent visuals.
Do not shade areas under velocity-time graphs.
Do not generate image assets during this pass.

concepts_taught: Gradient is vertical change divided by horizontal change.
A tangent estimates an instantaneous gradient on a curve.
Gradient sign gives direction and gradient magnitude gives the size of the rate.
misconceptions_addressed: A graph's drawn angle can be compared across different axis scales.
Any two points on a curve give the instantaneous gradient.
Negative gradient always means slowing down.
A horizontal velocity-time line means the object is stationary.
